utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. The Chamber will issue two rulings before we hear evidence from the witness. First, on the 22nd January, 2014, the accused filed a request for presence of counsel and questions to be posed to General Ratko Mladic, wherein the accused requests that Ratko Mladic's counsel be present during his testimony in these proceedings. On the 23rd of January, the Prosecution communicated via e-mail that it did not wish to respond to this request. The request is hereby granted. Next, the Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's submission on form of Karadzic's testimony filed on the 8th of January, 2014, which I will refer to in this oral ruling as "submission," in which the Prosecution requests the Chamber to disallow the accused to testify in a narrative form. By way of background, the Chamber recalls that on the 16th of December, 2013, the accused's legal advisor stated that the accused had originally planned on 32 hours of examination-in-chief and intended to request the Chamber to allow the accused's legal advisor to question the accused but subsequently decided that the accused should testify in narrative form so as to cut the estimated time in half and to save the time allocated to his Defence case. In the submission of order of witnesses for February and March 2014, which was filed on the 18th of December, 2013, the accused confirmed his intention to testify in narrative form. In its submission, the Prosecution argues that the accused's intention to testify in this specific form ignores the fact that such a decision falls within the Chamber's discretion pursuant to Rule 90 (F) of the Rules. The Prosecution also asserts that the accused's reliance on a single US case from 2011 is misconstrued. Furthermore, the Prosecution submits that it is speculative and unrealistic to claim that testifying by way of narrative could half the time otherwise estimated for the accused's examination-in-chief. It argues that contrary to the accused's assertion, testimony in question-and-answer form would in fact "facilitate the Prosecution to raise objections, assist the Chamber in exercising control over proceedings, and provide for clearer, more structured and more focussed testimony." The accused did not respond to the Prosecution's submission. The Chamber recalls its order on the procedure for the conduct of trial issued on the 8th of October, 2009, where it underscored its responsibility "to ensure that the trial is conducted in a fair and expeditious manner" in accordance with the Statute and the Rules with full respect for the rights of the accused. The Chamber also notes that Rule 90 (F) provides it with discretion to exercise control over the mode of interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence so as to, 1, make the interrogation and presentation effective for the ascertainment of the truth, and, number 2, avoid needless consumption of time. Furthermore, Rule 85 (B) sets out the procedure for examination-in-chief, requiring that "the party calling a witness to examine such witness in-chief ..." The Chamber notes that the accused's sole rationale for testifying in narrative form is saving the time allocated to his Defence case, referring to one domestic case. In the Chamber's view, this case has no direct bearing on the practice of this Tribunal. In any event, the accused has failed to articulate why this case should be considered in this specific instance. The question-and-answer format, which is the standard procedure for the examination of witnesses before the Tribunal, has been applied in this case throughout. The Chamber considers that this form generally produces structured and focussed testimony, facilitates the ability of the cross-examining, to raise timely objections where appropriate, and assists the Chamber in exercising control over the proceedings, therefore making the presentation of evidence effective for the ascertainment of the truth and avoiding unnecessary consumption of court time. In this light, the accused has failed to substantiate his contention that narrative testimony would be more effective and time-saving than the stand question-and-answer form. The Chamber can see no reason for departing from the well-established practice when it comes to the accused's testimony. Accordingly, the Chamber grants the Prosecution's request and instructs, number 1, the accused to testify in question-and answer form, and, number 2, his legal advisor to put questions to him during his own testimony. We'll bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will be now reading out the summary of Mr. Jevto Jankovic's statement in English. [In English] Jevto Jankovic was born on 9th of March, 1953, in the victim of Bistrica, Banja Luka municipality. Between 1977 and 2001, he was the investigating judge of the Banja Luka Lower Court, whereby together with his colleagues he was performing his duties on the basis of their own moral and professional qualities up to the beginning of the civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, during the war and after it - never on the basis of party membership. In addition, after the League of Communists, Jevto Jankovic was not a member of any political party. In the first multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, three leading parties emerged on the political scene: The SDA, as the party of the Muslims; the HDZ, the Croatian party; and the SDS, Serbian Democratic Party, as a party representing the political will of the Serbs. There were political confrontations between the SDA and HDZ on one hand, endeavouring in every manner possible for Bosnia to secede from Yugoslavia, and the SDS and other smaller pro-Yugoslav parties whose political activities were aimed at preserving the existing state of the SFRY and Bosnia and Herzegovina as a member of the federal state. By the beginning of 1991, members of the Party of Democratic Action and the BH Croatian Democratic Union joined paramilitary and terrorist organisations under the leadership of the chauvinist HDZ leadership in Croatia where the civil war was already underway and the same were involved in armed combat against regular Yugoslav People's Army, JNA. Jevto Jankovic conducted investigations on a monthly basis in about 50 cases where members of the security services found Muslims and Croats in possession of concealed military weapons and various explosive devices, in the respect that individuals, groups and even formations were armed in an organised manner and sent by leading members of the HDZ and SDA in the BH. On 30th July, 1992, following a report from the duty officer of the Banja Luka CJB, Jevto Jankovic led an on-site investigation at Manjaca where two detainees had died. Jevto Jankovic submitted a report to the relevant prosecutor, and to the extent he had been informed, the military policemen were tried before the relevant courts for this crime. Until the 22nd of August, 1992, the police duty service called me -- him and said that one of the -- or two bodies had been found in the general area of Knezevo and that an on-site investigation was needed. He personally saw the dispatches between the then-president of the republic, Radovan Karadzic, and the Minister of Interior, Mico Stanisic, which clearly stated that the perpetrators of the massacre at Koricanske Stijene should be found and tried before the relevant courts. As far as the crime at Koricanske Stijene is concerned, Jevto Jankovic states that it was committed by criminals selected and mobilised for this purpose, and that the people issuing the orders were from foreign intelligence services. Their aim was to portray the Serbs and legal organs of government as criminals. In July 1991 [sic], Jevto Jankovic gave a statement to The Hague investigators regarding the events at Koricanske Stijene, to an investigator from Pakistan. As the truth was not favourable to some foreigners in BH or to individuals in the Serbian criminal world, Jevto Jankovic was put under pressure and offered money to go to The Hague to testify for the Prosecution in the manner they wanted it. And that is the short summary. Now I would like to call the document, but prior to that, I would ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.text: My answer would be yes. And that is, indeed, what was done. Actually, many crimes were committed by both Serbs and Muslims and Croats, at least in the area that was relatively peaceful. We prosecuted all, irrespective of ethnic affiliations. Of course, within the realm of the possible. Hardly anybody knows the conditions under which we lived. Only we do. We didn't have electricity. People were on the move. utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC

The question of all questions was to transfer the war to Bosnia-Herzegovina and that is what is Stipe Mesic managed to do in cahoots with foreign intelligence services. And as the Bosnians would say, we knew that there would be trouble. As far as the front line is concerned, I can tell you in general terms there was fighting in the area of the so-called - no, it's not so-called - the Serb Krajina. And that was about 50 or 60 kilometres away from us. And then when the war spilled over to Bosnia-Herzegovina, then many front lines were opened like Vecici, Sijekovac, Kupres, not to enumerated all of them now. It depended on the period involved. I would need a lot of time. Some were about 30 kilometres away, others were about 60 kilometres away, and yet others 40 to 50 kilometres away. From us, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that that never happened. They didn't hush anything up. Even later on, when we get to Koricanske Stijene, this was not an investigation. This was investigative action, and that's why you perhaps don't understand this very well. Investigative action is action taken that is bare necessity in order not to destroy evidence which cannot be obtained at a later date. So it is a well-known fact that after the Serb Bosnia-Herzegovina was established, that is to say Republika Srpska, according to the constitution, according to the law, and according to all our regulations, regardless of who the perpetrator was, that person was prosecuted, of course, within the scope of our possibilities because it is a well-known thing that war was raging. There is was no electricity. There was no water. It was very difficult. I've already said a moment ago I don't even want to remember that. But whatever was possible was prosecuted. Many things could not have been dealt with because, thank God, everybody knows that a civilian could not disarm a soldier who had an automatic rifle or arrest a person who had a tank. That is only logical that that could not have been done. However, whatever could have been dealt with was dealt with, at least in the area of the town where I lived and where I worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause between the answer and your question, as well. Mr. Jankovic, I'm not sure I understood you in full. Could you tell us again the difference between the investigation and investigative action. What's the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a major difference, Mr. President. Investigative action is urgent by its very nature. And, according to the law that was then in force, if evidence is not obtained immediately, or right after something happened, later on, it cannot be obtained. Investigation, according to the laws that were in force then in our country, could be carried out only against known perpetrators at the proposal of the prosecutor's office or the prosecutor. So the prosecutor would have to file charges against a known perpetrator and then an investigation could start. Whereas, on-site investigation, autopsy, and some other urgent action is this investigative action, something that cannot be delayed. So that is how our law dealt with that. And then it was the investigating judge who carried out such investigative action. Now this is done by a prosecutor. So investigative action is only what is urgent and what has to be dealt with immediately. Evidence has to be collected as soon as possible or straight away. That is what I meant, and I hope that you understand me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it there. Yes, shall we continue.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please help us with this. Is this a second-instance judgement?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a judgement of the district court in Banja Luka. The number is 82/99, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness will have to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If you reading something, please read slowly because we have to hear it through interpreters. Yes, could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the proposal of the president of the Chamber, there is a judgement. The appeal is granted of the public prosecutor from Banja Luka, of the basic court in Banja Luka, case 6/93 from the 23rd of February, 1993. It is being overturned so the accused, Aleksic Sredo, on the basis of Article 151, paragraph 2, the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska, is being sentenced to one year and a half in prison and also he is being credited for the time he has already spent in detention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please slow down. Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at page 16. 3216 is the ERN number, the last digits of the ERN number of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a record, 625/92. The date is the 8th of November, 1992. Attempted murder on the 6th of November, 1992, around 2100 hours in Knezevo, the neighbourhood of Mahala, the street of Rahidan Madajlic [phoen] number 9. And murder was attempted. There was attempted murder against Fata Musanovic. I carried out the investigation and the on-site investigation was also attended by Vesna Rujovic [phoen], who was the deputy public prosecutor from Banja Luka; Milan Pajnovic [phoen], an inspector of the SJB of Banja Luka; and Srdjan Oljaca, a crime technician from the SJB of Banja Luka..

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear Dr. Karadzic because this was an on-site translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreters didn't catch up with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to see the last page, 229. The last digits are 3229.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question was, Mr. Jankovic: Do you know of a single case where our judicial authorities discriminated against perpetrators based on their ethnicity or the ethnicity of the victims?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I need to explain to the Trial Chamber. It was the reality, at least in the area of my court, and I have information that it was the same in the area of other courts of Republika Srpska, we prosecuted any known perpetrator. We were not able, of course, to prosecute unknown perpetrators, but we prosecuted perpetrators whenever they were known and whenever we knew where they were. Those were the basic principles. We did not prosecute more people of other ethnicities in favour of the Serbs. We prosecuted all criminals. That was the rule in practice, and we had instructions to act that way. I'd like to see here similar documents concerning Sarajevo or Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking here to extend remand by two months. Can you imagine this extension of remand for Sredo Aleksic in war time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was a judge able to request extension of remapped and who else was able to do that?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor could. I asked for this in -- in a request, in an application addressed to the Trial Chamber because I, as an investigating judge, could extend remand up to maximum of one month. This is for two months, so it was up to the trial chamber. Can you imagine my reckless valour in asking for this person to stay in remand for another two months?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We dealt with the cover page, third page, page 16, and page 34. Are we admitting only those four pages, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's been our practice, Mr. President, although we would prefer to have the entire filed admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll put those four pages marked for identification. We'll include page 21 as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D4239, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were an investigating judge for a long time. Can you tell us, especially concerning the war-time-period, how did your investigations proceed? How were they finalised? How did various trial chambers make decisions based on your investigations?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to talk about myself, but I won't have another opportunity. I majored in criminology and I have been working in the judiciary of Republika Srpska for 40 years, first of all, in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, later in Republika Srpska. After my investigations, indictments were issued, confirmed, and convictions were made without any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 1D9624.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson and Mr. Tieger, I'm not sure we heard from the witnesses or through written evidence as to the qualifications or professional requirements for a person to be appointed a judge, investigating judge. Otherwise, I would like you to deal with this issue with the witness briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I also don't recall that, although we have had some evidence about military judges but not the civilian ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue. In particular, I note the passage from this witness's statement, it's third paragraph: "I performed my duties as investigating judge on the basis of my moral and professional qualities." I take it you followed. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will deal with that through the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, first of all, do you remember this case, Bavarcic?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I dealt with many cases. Can you give me more details apart from the name and the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 25.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I see it's qualified murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 25. Is it now clearer what this case is about? Whose document is it?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mine. This is my decision to carry out an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the act in question?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This offender, Bosko Bavarcic, perpetrated the crime of aggravated robbery and qualified murder. Article 151, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the trial judgement, page 12 in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who are the injured parties by ethnicity? You don't have to give us the names.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall. I need to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we see the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we zoom in?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This perpetrator was found guilty because, on the 6th of May, 1992, in Donji Vakuf, he entered the house of Hamda Karasin [phoen]. You see that the injured parties were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And under B?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of June, 1992, in Donji Vakuf, intending to kill Fuad Avdic. Again injured party is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This area was no longer ours but the front line was on the border. I just want the Trial Chamber to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The question was not heard without microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was convicted and sentenced to two years of imprisonment for murder and aggravated robbery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear my question. I asked how this was qualified and what the judgement was.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The sentence was five years. That's what matters. And the crime was aggravated murder.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 3 now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what is this document? What does the appeal judgement say?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I see that this is the higher court in Banja Luka, where it was sent by the district court and then it was sent back to the district court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Part of the appeal was granted. So Bosko Bavarcic originally charged with murder and other crimes was sentenced to eight years. So his sentence was raised from five to eight years imprisonment during the war, during the fiercest fighting, and it was done by a civilian court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is the appeal judgement of 1993 [Realtime transcript read in error "1992"].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 6. It is missing from the record that the appeal judgement was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is his application to reduce the sentence?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: And the court decided that his request to reduce his sentence has no grounds and is rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark for identification the first page, pages 3, 6, 12, and 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And 25, of course. Yes. Shall we assign a number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D4240, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, if I may suggest that 3, 4, and 5, because that's the entirety of the trial Judgement; in fact, the appeal judgement, three pages of the appeal judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have no difficulty with that. We'll add page 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will skip the next case causing general danger. The perpetrator, a Serb, was again punished but I have no time. Thank you, Your Excellencies. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jankovic, before you are cross-examined, probably you remember my question. Could you tell us about the qualification or professional requirements to be appointed as a judge at the court at -- at -- at the time before the war or during the war? That also includes an investigating judges' qualification as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You will hear now. I am one of the rare people who graduated exclusively from professional schools. I finished the school of internal affairs in Kamenica, the higher criminology school in Zemun, and my average grade was 4.92. I graduated from law school. I worked for a long time as a crime investigations inspector and passed the bar exam. After that, I became an investigating judge in 1977 and worked in that post until 2002. In 2002, without any precedent in international legal practice, I was accused of obstructing the work of the prosecutor and the high commissioner removed me from office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber was only interested in knowing the qualification for you to be appointed as a judge before the war. We are not going to deal with -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, the qualifications that I just enumerated, you won't find many people who have that many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may clarify. Mr. Jankovic, before you were elected to the court, did you have to pass the bar exam?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said I passed the bar exam, all within record times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And your grade was 4.92?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That was my grade at the criminology school in Zemun. After that, I worked as a crime investigations inspector, and after that, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There's a mistake. The grade should be 9.42. My last question: When you said you had no party affiliation, did anyone ask you to join any political party? Or more specifically the SDS, in order to be able to continue in your job?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was in the movement, that is well known, but I was not a member of any party. I was a candidate of the SDS for the chief of SUP in Banja Luka, if anyone is interested. But only as a candidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were there also judges who didn't pass the bar examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, that could not happen. Your Honour, Mr. President, nowadays judges and prosecutors in their wondrous country of Bosnia-Herzegovina are much less qualified and much less able because they were elected by incompetent foreigners and criminals. It's difficult to become a judge -- just let me finish. You will see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, that's -- I was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will listen to you, but I am right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was interested in the system that was in practice during the war or before the war. Thank you, Mr. Jankovic. As you have noted, your evidence in-chief has been admitted in its most part in writing; that is, your witness statement in lieu of your oral testimony. And now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you just testified at page 27 that you became an investigating judge in 1977. You included that information in your statement at paragraph 2 as well. But isn't it true that you only graduated from law school in 1983 and you passed the bar examination in 1985?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, that's impossible. You see, I graduated from law school in 19 ... 19 ... I became, in 1977, judge, and graduated from law school five or six years earlier. You do the sums. I have my diploma. I didn't know you would ask me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: You are wasting your time proving my qualifications. There is written proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at some of that written proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we have P6525, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: What you will see when it comes up is a letter from the Banja Luka public prosecutor to the Banja Luka War Presidency dated 6 July 1992 with a list of candidates proposed for the position of deputy prosecutor and judicial appointments in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we go first to B/C/S page 4, English page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So here you'll see a heading which says list of candidates for the position of judge at the lower court in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now if we could go to the next page in B/C/S and page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: There, near the top, by number 12 with a circle around it you have your name --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If you'd let me finish. With all of your personal information, and it says: "Graduated in 1983, passed the bar examination in 1985, Serb, judge at this court since 1989?" Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, possibly. Then it must be 1987, not 1977, but 1987. Yes, this is possible. I apologise. I really didn't know I would be asked this question. It's possible that this is true. 1985, 1989. This is true. This is correct. I made a mistake because it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Right. So you've increased your -- in your sworn testimony today, and in your statement, you've increased the length of your judicial career from approximately 12 years to approximately 24 years. You've effectively doubled the length of that career; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of math, that's right. I was judge from 1987. Maybe I made a mistake, but it was not deliberate. In any case, I was investigating judge for a long time, and I was a crime investigations inspector for a long time as well. Both are true. I have been working since -- I worked from 1972 as a crime investigations inspector not as many years as I said, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to your statement where you say that you were suspended from your position as a judge on 23 May 2002 by the Office of the High Representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 25857, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Here you can see a copy of the decision that suspended you from your position as a judge. I'd like you to look at page 2 below reasons for suspension. There you can see that it says that it is alleged that Jevto Jankovic has repeatedly failed to uphold the rule of law and the OHR gave several reasons for its view that this took place. Under paragraph (a), you'll see failing to act in an impartial and professional manner towards the prosecution. And another reason, in paragraph (b) says that in your capacity as investigating judge you improperly released defendant from pre-trial detention. Now that's a correct understanding of the reasonings for your suspension; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, Mr. President, I have this decision. I don't know if you can hear me. I had that decision, and I wanted to show it to you. To put it quite simply, this is a decision without precedent in international law. My life and my entire career, which was 30 years at that time. Look, without any signature, it just says Wolfgang Petritsch, 23rd May, 2002, High Representative. So anyone could have written this. Without the English translation, without any signature, this decision was simply put out in the media and I was forbidden access to the court-house. Already by then, an independent judicial commission had been established and when I called him international criminal, the president of that chamber stopped me. His name is -- let me -- let me see. This is how much I've forgotten these things. It's an Englishman. I'll remember, if you let me find it. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, my question was simply whether this was a correct understanding of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object on grounds of relevance. Because when you look at the reasons -- looking at the first reason, the second, and the third they have nothing to do with his conduct during the war. So we -- I don't believe that it's relevant to any of the issues as to his testimony concerning how he handles his judicial duties during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is clearly relevant to the witness's credibility as well as the statement that he made. In his statement about, I believe it says performing his duties as investigative judge on the basis of his moral and professional qualities up to the beginning of civil in Bosnia, during the war, and after it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, and he also comments on his dismissal in para 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6608, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: One other question, Mr. Jankovic. You became a member of the SDS in 1997; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. I never was a member. But can I respond to this, Mr. President? Malcolm Simmons is the name of the man. If I can answer this question to you. It is very instructive for the sake of the profession, not because of Jevto Jankovic. So let me simplify this. I was accused here because of a woman called Maric, Svetlana, that I was obstructing her work. So let me explain this. I was in your seat, Svetlana Maric was the prosecutor, and a man accused of trafficking in women was the accused. And I was accused of obstructing the work of the prosecutor. Nowhere in the world can this be the case. The prosecutor can obstruct the procedure or the defence, but not the other way around. That's why I took this document along to show it to you. I worked conscientiously. However, in order to remove me from my position what was done was that I was denigrated in the eyes of my colleagues. So this woman is now the president of a -- a criminal law chamber in -- in Bosnia, whereas I was removed on these very grounds. And this was the reason why the prosecutor should, in fact, issue an indictment against Wolfgang Petritsch. Can you imagine the High Representative finding an insignificant judge obstructing allegedly somebody's work? Nobody could release anyone from detention other than the investigating judge. So what was this? This was mere propaganda. And many people in my unfortunate country of Bosnia-Herzegovina fell victim to this propaganda. And among those who stand trial, 90 to 95 per cent are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered the question and I think we heard from you sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you were interviewed by representatives of my office, the Office of the Prosecutor, in Banja Luka, on 21st of July, 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: If that's B.A. Nasar from Pakistan, if that's the man, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Did you tell the truth on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I always spoke the truth. There can only be some legal differences. Now the decision you've just shown me is a decision without precedent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We're not talking --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: And you -- you have demonstrated it here as proof against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We're not talking about that decision anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: What I'd like to look at is 65 ter number 25926, which is a copy of the transcript of that interview which took place on 21 July 2001. And if we could look at English page 17; B/C/S page 15 please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And here you will see the question asked to you: "You were never a member of SDS, for example?" Your answer was: "Yes, in 1997." That was the truth; right? Not what you've just told us today?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. That's not true. I don't know how this came about. I never was a member. Had I been a member of any party, I would have been a member of the leadership. I would have partaken in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now in your witness statement you said at paragraph 8 that: "The SDS leadership in Banja Luka proposed me and put me up as a non-partisan candidate for the post of chief of the Banja Luka public security centre when they assumed power based on the election results." But isn't it true that you believed that the head of the CSB in Banja Luka would have to answer to the SDS, that the head would be controlled by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The head was not controlled by the SDS. I was not a member of the SDS. I was, indeed, nominated as a candidate. You said yourself that a logical interpretation of my sentence would be that I was put forward as a non-partisan candidate. Let me repeat this: Had I been a member of the SDS, I would have been a member of the leadership. I would at the very least have been a deputy in the Assembly. I had not attended a single meeting of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not ashamed of it. I could have been a member of the SDS but I'm just telling you that I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I think we are in agreement that you were not a member of the SDS until at least 1997. But you believed, at the time, in 1992, that the SDS would interfere in the work of the head of the CSB. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. You can't put it that way. There's no logic to it. So I was not in 1991. But I was in 1997. And already the head was elected. And that was the only intention that I had, the only aspiration that I had, nothing else. I didn't need a professional function of any sort to be a member of the party or of a party. But I could have been a member of the SDS. It's a party of the Serbian people, and I am a part of that. I'm telling you formally I was not. I was a part of the movement. Had I been, I would have been promoted. I would have taken up certain positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, our time is limited and I would prefer that you give focussed and precise answers to the question I'm asking. Now, if we could look at this document that is on the screen, English page 31 --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you in quite precise terms that I was not, and you can do whatever you want. It's easy for me to confirm this. I can bring over 5.000 people who will testify to the fact that I was not. That I was never putting up a public appearances. If you know this, then this must be some sort of a novelty.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It's B/C/S page 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were you a member? Did you become a member of SDS in 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, in order for me to become a member of the SDS, I would have to pay the membership fee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about this. Somebody may have applied on my behalf. There were such cases, but I myself did not pay a single penny towards the membership fee, and I never considered myself to be a SDS member. There were some friends of mine who were SDS members and said, Well, you belong with us. But formally speaking, I was not there. I did not pay a single penny toward the membership fee and that's proof of the fact that I was not a member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just asked you because the transcript was not clear whether you said you were a member in 1997. It's still -- So you were not a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Maybe somebody applied for my membership without me wanting it. But I would have had to pay the membership fee at any rate, which I did not do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I'll leave it at that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Looking at this page on your screen you'll see the question is asked to you: "Did you believe that the head of the CSB in Banja Luka would have to answer to the SDS, that the head would be controlled by the SDS? Your answer: "Yes. Well, a simple calculation. After the multi-party elections first party, the top party in this area was SDS. And they naturally chose the most important positions or functions. "Q. And did you believe that they would also interfere in the work of the head of the CSB? "A. Of course, each party wanted their men. That's math." That's what you said on that day during that interview, and that was the truth, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I read this out again and then you draw your logical inferences: JJ: No, no, no, all three of us were non-partisan candidates. Think about it, the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party, put forward myself and Stojan and Milovan Jancic for the head of the public security centre. That's the Banja Luka region. But as non-partisan candidate, as professionals, am I quite clear? So, what I said neither Stojan, nor Jancic nor I were members. And as for the rest, every party has its own set of rules. And that was the very reason why I avoided getting affiliated with any party. And I told you that had I joined them I would probably have been part of the SDS leadership. What does membership mean to you? Being a member --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: All you just did was read a different section of the transcript. What I asked you was the portion that I read about your belief that the head of the CSB in Banja Luka would have to answer to the SDS and your belief that they would interfere in the work of the head of the CSB, that was the truth, that you spoke that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, no. That's -- the SDS head did not report to the SDS president but to the national assembly, regardless of the party that he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You meant the CSB head, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, the head of the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This would be a good time for a break, if Your Honour is inclined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What -- page number for the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: English page 31; B/C/S page 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So where can we see "no, no, no," in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I think that part may be on a previous page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under number 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you find the passage in English, "no, no, no." "JJ: No, no, no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All three of us were non-partisan candidates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you let us know after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break. I was told it's on page 29, but it says, "no, yay, no." Probably maybe that. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And before I begin, I can also confirm that it's our understanding as well that English page 29, lines 23 to 27 is the translation of the portion you were asking about before. One other question, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Sorry to interrupt you. But before we continue, I'm coming back to the exhibit issue. Yes. I agree with -- the Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson that unless the document is something that has been produced for the purpose of current proceedings, we have a basis to -- to admit document as long as it has been commented upon or confirmed by the witness. So on that basis, we'll admit the document. Yes, 1D9622. Shall we assign a number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4241, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: One other question, Your Honour, in light of some translations that became available at the end of the day on Friday, I would ask for some extra time to deal with some of those exhibits. I don't think I'll need more than an extra 30 minutes but I just wanted to request that in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Jankovic, we've been looking at this transcript from this interview. I asked you earlier today whether you answered those questions truthfully. Your response at page 34 was "I always spoke the truth."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would also like to look at page 91 in the English of this document; B/C/S page 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, on this page, you say, and I quote: "I was honest. Not because of you, but for the God. Try and find one example or a case where I didn't tell you the truth and I knew the truth?" So I just want to verify that you were telling the truth that day on 2001 when you spoke to the OTP; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. You removed the document. Mr. President, can we go back to that "no, no." I read out a very important sentence -- I read a very important sentence in there and I'd like all of you to see it if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, if you could concentrate on the current question. If necessary, Mr. Karadzic will lead you there again. But where can we see this passage, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I believe it's on page 91 of the English, lines 22 to 24. I'm sorry, this doesn't correspond to what I have. It's a page with ERN L0049756. I think it may be on the next page of this. For some reason the pagination -- the pagination is off. It will be page 92 of the English. It looks like it's at line 14 to 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you confirm with -- the page -- B/C/S page number with the witness, whether he can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you see the passage that I just read to you where you said: "I was honest. Not because of you, but for the God," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, say it. I can't see it here. Let's go slowly. That's the beginning where I have it. What's the line number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It should be ERN L0072359.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It may be -- it should be line 24 on the -- the current page that is showing, it should be line 24.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see this: Okay, I don't hold anything against you. I was honest. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That's it. That appears to be page 80?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I believe I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So my question was: On that day in 2001, you answered the questions from the Office of the Prosecutor truthfully; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. But I don't know how the interpreter interpreted it, and what was recorded. I'm not Bismark. I can't read this all at once and confirm it. I can tell you that I was honest but I don't know if it was honestly reflected here. But go back to that case and you'll see how the meaning changed there. Can we go back to the point where I was being asked about my membership in SDS in 1997. And I said that there was no logic to it. How -- why would I have been a member in 1997 if I wasn't a member in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, as Mr. President indicated previously, Mr. Karadzic will have an opportunity to ask you additional questions if it's necessary. Right now I want to ask you about your witness statement, paragraph 7, where you say: "In the lower court, that is to say as investigating judge, my colleagues and I worked slowly on the basis of the law at this time. We were never under influence by anyone on how to conduct investigations or other activities when investigating and punishing crimes. I'm saying this because those perpetrating crimes were the same for us, regardless of the ethnicity or religion. I remember that as investigating judge, I was engaged in work where we tried more Serbs for crimes committed against non-Serbs." Now I'd like to look at the transcript of your interview again, English page 34 and B/C/S page 30. You will see the question you were asked: "The question again is: Did you find in your work during this war time in 1992 it was impossible for you to fulfil your obligations to investigate and punish these crimes by Serbs against Muslims and Croats because of the pressure from other people?" Your answer was: "Yes. That's mathematically correct. What do you think, that I was allowed in put in prison someone who carried an automatic weapon, by just issuing a piece of paper, a decision" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do we have that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make sure that we have the page before reading out ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, line 3. Let's check the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's page 29 in the B/C/S, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what was entered in the transcript, what the Prosecutor read out, cannot be found on this page. And yet we have it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: What I read into the transcript is at the top of the page on English e-court page 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about B/C/S page. You referred to line 23 of this page? Not -- not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Let me just verify. It appears that in uploading, the pagination has changed from what I have in my hard copy to what's in e-court. Right. I believe that it is -- it is this section that was previously referred to on page 29. It begins with "panaravno [phoen]."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the line number as well. Yes, what was -- what's the line number?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It wasn't that page. It's on a page with ERN L0072311.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem is that the -- the ERN in my hard copy is at the top of each page. And in this version that was uploaded, it appears at different points on different pages, and so the actual pagination of the document differs. Would it be possible to have just a brief break so that we could correct that and upload an improved version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we rise for five minutes? Would that be sufficient? Or you need more?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That will be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.25 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. File, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for your patience and apologies for the error.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We were looking at the transcript of your interview at English page 34 and B/C/S page 30. And the passage that I read to you was: "Did you find in your work during this war time in 1992, it was impossible for you to fulfil your obligations to investigate and punish these crimes by Serbs against Muslims and Croats because of the pressure from other people?" And your answer was: "Yes. That's mathematically correct. What do you think, that I was allowed to put in prison someone who carried an automatic weapon, by just issuing a piece of paper, a decision?" That's what you said in 2001 and that was your truthful belief at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. The translation is not correct here. Possibly I said that it was mathematically correct that we prosecuted all. I don't know where this comes from. I mean, maybe I talked to him about the difficulties involved. Of course, that's only natural. I exposed myself to that a thousand time. That's simply the way it was. Can you imagine there is a war raging, everybody has a rifle, a tank, and then you send them into custody because of some crime. I had personal problems because I did actually do that, and I jeopardised myself in that way. But what you read out here, that somebody exerted pressure against me, I don't know who you meant. That somebody could have exerted pressure against me. I was the civilian authorities then, the judiciary authorities. If you mean the SDS, no. If you mean the president of the republic, no. I don't know who have you in mind, who was it that could have exerted pressure against me. You should have told me about that, that somebody was exerting pressure against me. Who? There were foreign intelligence services that were pressuring me. And a lot of us were being pressured by them. Of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: -- not everybody's ideal -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Let's look at a passage just a little bit further on. It's page 36 in the English and pages 31 to 32 of the B/C/S, which might clarify this. Here you said: "It's not that I had a pressure of military authorities to process cases. The time was that perpetrators of murders at those times or at that time were unknown." You went on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This version in the English appears to be suffering from the same problem as before. Oh, no, it's actually in lines 17 to 19 where he says: "It's not that I had pressure of military authorities to process cases. The time was that perpetrators of murders at those times at that time were unknown."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I believe that's the correct page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Jankovic, you go on to say: "Or if they were known, they were at the front line and I didn't -- they were not within my range. I didn't have any jurisdiction over them. So simply put, I couldn't and I didn't dare - you choose what you want - to process the murder cases in which victims were Muslims and Croats." A few lines down, you asked the question: "My question is - you say" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the next page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You were asked the question: "My question is - you say that soldiers would be at the front line and outside of your jurisdiction. The front lines were not in Afghanistan, they were a matter of a few hours at most from Banja Luka. Why couldn't you order ... what would happen if you ordered the police to bring you the suspect from the front line?" Your answer was: "First, I couldn't have done it even in theory. "Q. Explain that. "A. I told you the reason. I was a civilian person. How could you issue an order to a military person or policeman, police person?" Now does that clarify the context for you in which you gave your answer?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your questions at all. But it is correct that I, as a civilian judge, could not arrest a soldier who had committed a crime because in the meantime a military court was established, so that was under the jurisdiction of the military court. And I don't see what you find unclear there. So I'm a civilian judge, and where crimes were committed in Banja Luka, well, yes, there were civilian -- there were Serb criminals who killed a Muslim or a Croat in order to gain some kind of advantage. But it was hard to find perpetrators because everybody had a rifle. And there was a military situation there, and we were dealing with the front line, and with crime, too. Now, I'm just explaining this to you. So I can explain this to you within the framework of the authority that I had. I did not have any kind of military powers. I had civilian powers. We arrested criminals. You saw a moment ago how many people were sentenced. So find an example like that to the contrary. I mean, since you've asked me, but you did not ask me about this man who abused me for ten hours. He had come from Pakistan and this was a holiday dedicated to a great saint, and I was thinking in my head, God, God, and then I asked him. Maybe he wrote that. How can I arrest someone who has a tank? And he'd say, Yes. And then he'd take a break. And then he consulted some Serb criminal. And then he'd come back again. And again, he would abuse Jevto Jankovic. I mean, a policeman from Lahore. And then this other policeman from Karachi, he's a Pakistani too, but he is civilian -- but he was civilised. I don't want to lie before God. And then -- I mean, we don't want a man from Pakistan coming in, rather have someone from Norway. I mean, in Pakistan there are bombs falling every day. I mean, I'm not saying they're not a good people in general. But anyway -- but maybe I did have this discussion with him, but I mean, he abused me for ten hours. For him, I am an intellectual and he is a policeman, and he asked me about two Muslim victims out of 30.000 Serb victims, and he didn't me about that. That's it, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you've also -- you've also claimed in your statement at paragraph 15 that the investigator pressured you into giving false testimony. Now you've just said that he abused you for ten hours. I have a copy of the entire transcript of that interview in your language. When we get to the next break, I'd like to give you the opportunity to review that transcript, and when we return, you can show us where in the interview you were abused or pressured into giving false testimony. Would that be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 7, you say on 30th July, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. We did not hear anything from the witness with regard to the previous question and we're already moving on to the next question. This, "no," merely, is not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that your -- not your answer, Mr. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, that was my answer. Do you understand that? I mean -- well, Mr. President, I have no reason to exaggerate or to lie about anything. So, I mean, there are always legal intricacies and there are always leading questions, and there's always provocative questions that exist in the past and that will exist in the future. So I am telling the truth. So I'm telling you the man abused me for ten hours. Please, may I? I'm addressing you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember the question by Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember the question. And I gave him an answer that I was abused and that I did not say that because there's no need for me to say that kind of thing and I have no motive for saying that kind of thing. Now, how he calculated these questions of his and answers of mine technically, well, I know that technically nowadays you can do anything. So I'd fall silent when he would put his questions and I'd wonder, God, what have I done wrong? He doesn't know the situation in our country. He doesn't know the circumstances involved, and he's asking about Muslim victims. Only about Muslim victims. And then I saw that -- I mean, how I do put this? He is one-sided, interested in one question only, as if we did not have other obligations, other problems, just to take care of who would get killed. People get killed in a war especially in a civil war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you listen to the question and answer the question, please. I will leave it to you. Please continue, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, what I asked you was whether you would be willing to review the transcript at the next break and tell us where in the interview you believe that you were abused, or where in the interview you believe that you were pressured into giving false testimony. Because I would submit to you that nowhere in that interview do you ever complain about your treatment, nor do you claim that you were being pressured into false testimony. Are you willing to show us where in the transcript you believe this was happening?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This transcript is very long. I would need at least two days to read it and analyse each and every word. That is quite understandable. An interview of ten hours you cannot read that in a minute. Now as to whether this was done -- do you understand what I'm telling you? This man came. He asked about Muslim victims, about two cases. I mean, from Pakistan. He is abusing me. He is hollering at me. He is stopping the proceedings. Going out. Coming back. I'm silent because I don't know what to answer. What would that be but abuse? And now you're asking me why I did not sign in front of him that he had abused me. Nobody can function without logic. A judge, a prosecutor, a lawyer. And what I'm being asked is illogical. So I don't have a motive. I don't -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I take it that your answer is no, you're not willing to look at this over the next break?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am willing. I'm not evading any kind of question or answer, regardless of who or what this is related to and whether it affects me or somebody else. I am willing. But I'm telling you that this is logical. I see that it's put in a leading fashion too. I told you I have been involved in this practice for 40 years, and I have a degree in criminology. And, I mean, who can remember what they were asked 40 years ago or 30 years ago or 20 years ago? One's mind cannot work that way. I'm not Bismark.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In your --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm addressing the --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: -- Chamber. I'm going to answer each and every one of your questions if it is short, clear, and precise, regardless of whether if affects me or anyone else. But just tell me what. I don't understand these questions. They are leading questions. And I live in civil law, continental law.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about paragraph 7 of your statement where you say that: "On the 30th of July, 1992, following a report from the duty officer of the Banja Luka CJB, public security centre, I led an on-site investigation at Manjaca where two detainees had died."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Paragraph number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Of his statement. It's the last -- the last paragraph of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In that paragraph you say that you investigated, and at the end you say: "I submitted a report to the relevant prosecutor and as far as I know, the military policemen were tried before the relevant court for this crime." Now what you failed to mention is that this trial did not take place until 2007 under the auspices of different authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What you said is correct. As for the action that I took, I can say, loud and clear, I carried out only the on-site investigation and compiled the record. I could not do anything else even if I --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That actually goes beyond what I'd asked you. I'd like to turn your attention --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not submit a report. This was written by a man who's not a lawyer. I compiled a record. I did not submit a report. And in such circumstances, that was a masterpiece too. On the other side there weren't many on-site investigations and there were killings, murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. This was written by a man who is not a lawyer. What did you mean? And that your statement was written by a man who is not a lawyer and you do not agree with it. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. This is the way it was. I just compiled a record on the on-site investigation. And that was submitted to the prosecutor's office in charge. And now these prosecutor's offices, because of the changes that took place in our country, sometimes it was military and sometimes it was civilian. So what -- the prosecutor is correct. This was prosecuted only later, subsequently. So at the time when I took action, I did not know who the perpetrator was. I mean, I just compiled a record. I went up there and I had pictures taken, and I realised that this had to do with the killing of two persons and the identification of these persons. So as far as I was concerned as investigating judge, that was that. That was that investigative action that I was explaining to you, Mr. President. Whereas the investigation could take place only when the name of the perpetrator is known and also at the request of the prosecutor's office. Just like you cannot do anything before you get the indictment. So that's the way it was. I was not in the position of the prosecutor's office. I compiled a record and that shows that we did not conceal anything. I could have not compiled a record as well, but I did that for moral and professional reasons. I don't know if I'm being clear, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention now to the 21 August 1992 massacre at Koricanske Stijene. You were one of three investigating judges in Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And there -- and there was duty roster for the three investigative judges whereby each of you would be on duty to receive new cases for approximately one week at a time; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a roster, but I know what you want to ask me, so ask me and I'll give you a concrete explanation. Two were Croats, and people asked me that they not go because their lives would be in jeopardy so that's why I went, at their request. Zoran Lipovac - I'll give you the name - he is now a judge in the constitutional court. Ask me everything and I will tell you everything. Briefly and clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Rather than guessing what I'm going to ask, I'd like you to answer my questions as I ask them. My question was going to be: You were assigned to be the investigating judge because you were on-call or on duty that day; right?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was on duty and I was the only investigating judge. There you go. Realistically speaking. On paper there were three of us. These two men did not come to work because they had not responded to their military obligation call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: As investigating judge, you were in charge of the on-site investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You could give orders to the police at the crime scene, such as to take photographs or otherwise document the scene, to conduct forensic investigations, autopsies, exhumations, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In legal conditions, yes. But in illegal conditions, I did something and now I have to explain all of this here. I did whatever I could under these circumstances. I was an investigating judge, and, yes, I'm going to answer your further questions. As for exhumations, that was out of the question. That could not be carried out. As for autopsies, a man did try, Dr. Vodovnik, he tried to deal with a few corpses but then he went to Slovenia. So even autopsies could not be carried out. I did issue orders orally, and I can explain to you how and why. But I'm repeating, once again, it was only investigative action, not an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you also had the power to order the police to bring witnesses to you for questioning and also to identify and arrest perpetrators; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have the authority to arrest perpetrators in that situation. That was impossible. First of all, that was the first major case --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Sorry. Not -- not to arrest perpetrators yourself but to order the police to do so.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The procedure was totally different. There is procedure everywhere. Mr. President, please. Do pay attention to this. Until then, we call this mass killings, multiple killings, and so on. And until then, it was the State Security Service that carried out on-site investigations for that. And the investigating judge was only in charge of autopsy and exhumation. So it was this action that could be taken by the investigating judge. The SDB took care of all the rest according to Article 154, paragraph 2. Once I went out to deal with this and -- and went back and then I was there --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was there for two hours. And I was never on the scene any longer than that. And I can explain all of that to you if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Between 1500 and 1700 hours. How long is that? Four hours, yes, yes. In the middle of the month of August. I mean -- oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd object to the accused feeding answers to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it was a translation. Transcript said two hours and Mr. Karadzic asked four hours. I think that was it. But let me come back to your answer, Mr. Jankovic. Mr. File asked you this, I'll quote: "You could give orders to the police at the crime scenes, such as to take photographs or otherwise document the scene, to conduct forensic investigations, autopsies, exhumations, et cetera?" Now this is your answer: "Yes. In legal conditions, yes. But in illegal conditions, and I did something and now I have to explain all of this here." Do you remember having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly. But I'll repeat it for you again. Very simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. What did you mean "in illegal conditions"? What did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Abnormal conditions, that's what I meant. I could not take any action realistically except for what I could see with my very own eyes. From the top of the rock, I could see this pile of corpses. So I would have needed a lot of equipment in order to identify these persons, to get them out to an accessible spot, identify them, and then take further legal actions. So, yes, I did issue orders, and that is correct, on the spot. Srdjan Oljaca and Vukovac Branko [phoen], and Sukalo, Radovan took photographs using a camera, and that was the only thing that could have been do then. You know, he took a camera and took pictures because that was in this abyss. You could see for about 50 metres or perhaps 100 metres, you could see it with your own eyes, but it was inaccessible. So this was photographed. And the SFOR broke into SUP and took this, and later on, others even sold this. So that was an on-site investigation that started but it did not end. Since I was very busy, I was the only the investigating judge realistically speaking at the time, I authorised the crime inspector, and I could do that at the time, to continue the on-site investigation with Dr. Vodovnik and other persons. However they compiled a record. They returned and soon after that, he went to Slovenia and he said, It's there in my record. Don't count on me. I'm going to Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Later on, you said: "As for exhumations, that was out of the question." Why was it so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because we did not have a single pathologist left. Aco Vodovnik was the last one. And exhumations, you know, that implies extraction of bodies, identification of bodies, and we didn't have a single person who would do that. And to make it technically possible we needed a crane, and the crane needed to be brought between rocks. That is to say, we didn't need a crane. We needed horses, because with horses we could drag these bodies out. First they had to be dug out, and then hauled up to a place where identification could be conducted. You can check this. Until Dr. Karan appeared, and he appeared much later, we didn't have anyone. So from 1991, from Aco Vodovnik until Zeljko Karan appeared, we did not have a single forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 58, line 1, I believe there's some confusion. The witness was talking about video footage, not photographs. I should like to ask the Trial Chamber to clarify what kind of recording was made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The crime technicians video camera was used. Radovan Sukalo, Vukovac Branko, and Mr. Oljaca filmed the entire area, whatever could be seen. They could not descend to the bottom because it was -- they would be risking their lives.
