utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could please look at the -- at 65 ter 25926, which is on the screen currently. English page 12; B/C/S page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Here, near the top of the page you say: "I could have ordered the police to identify, to find perpetrators of such a crime, and in case it is urgent" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please provide the reference in the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only heard it now. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It's page 10 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it the passage where I say that's what we call investigative action or preliminary investigation procedures? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You say: "I could have ordered the police to identify, to find perpetrators of such a crime, and in case it is urgent, or it was urgent, to arrest them and to bring up charges against them ..." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. The truth is different. I was not able to. I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So you were not telling the complete truth to the investigators that day.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what that investigator gave you and wrote to you. But I maintain to you that I only carried out preliminary investigating procedures. I, as the investigating judge, could not order the police. There is a concern procedure in place. I could only compile a record. The record is given to the prosecutor, and the prosecutor could order the police to identify perpetrators, and once they are known, they should be subjected to investigation. I really don't know what language to speak in. It's perfectly clear to me. But I can't make it clear to you. I could not order the police directly to arrest anyone. I was an investigating judge conducting preliminary investigative actions and I make it available to the prosecutor. The prosecutor writes a request to the police and says, Please, identify perpetrators of this multiple murder at Koricanske and only once the perpetrators are identified can the investigation begin. That was the procedure. Then and now and ten years from now, I will keep saying the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a few brief questions about your investigation. The day after the massacre, i.e., 22 August 1992, you attempted to travel to the crime site with an investigative team only to be turned away by a policeman in Skender Vakuf or the town that was renamed Knezevo before you arrived at the scene. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. You see what happens with a formulation like that. It's like in English. Eat shoots and leaves, one coma makes the whole difference. I came on 22nd August, 1992, to carry out these preliminary investigative actions, not investigation, I repeat, with the same police team on the 22nd and the 23rd of August. I approached the policeman, the policeman recognised me and told me, Jevto, it is not one or two bodies. There are many bodies there. Those who were going towards Travnik. I told the police, We are in danger. Let's go back. Plus there was shooting over there. We returned by night and then the duty officer told me, Tomorrow morning, you have to go to the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, to clarify, it was the policeman who told you it was dangerous and turned you away.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He did not turn us back. I made the decision when I heard that report. Plus, I could hear the shooting and the shells falling. I made the decision because only two days before that, my colleague, Gordana Radojko [phoen], a prosecutor, took off her jacket only to find there was bullet-hole in it. He gave me that piece of information, and I decided that we should turn bark. He would not have been able to make me turn back because I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This police officer told you that the victims were probably part of a convoy of Muslim refugees; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: He told me there were many bodies there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: And we knew - please let me finish - we knew that a convoy from various places used that route. Those people were listed. It was a disgrace for the Serbs. We didn't need that. I can't understand the OTP for believing that somebody wanted to hush this up. I can never accept that. Every reasonable person condemned this crime. These people were accompanied by a list. The list was in the possession of the UNPROFOR, the Muslim side, the Croatian side, and the International Red Cross --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Mr. Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: So there were six lists, six copies of the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: To put it simply, you were able to conclude on the 22nd of August that people who had been killed at Koricanske Stijene were people of Muslim ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know that on the 22nd, until I came out to the scene. Later on, I made that conclusion after seeing the list. I didn't know it then. Please, I'm a lawyer, and you are a lawyer. You are a serious lawyer. I described to you the sequence of actions like in a chess game. My first move was to come out to the scene. I tried on the 22nd. I came to the centre of Knezevo. It's 30 kilometres more to Knezevo and we could already hear shells falling. And this man, the policeman, told me there are many bodies there. And when I came up there finally, I found one man. I cannot still tell his name because of things in my country. But I put the man in my own car and took him to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you page 45 in the English and page 40 in the B/C/S of the transcript of your interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It's actually page 46 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You were asked the question, this is at lines 8 to 10 in the English: "Were you able to conclude then on the 22nd of August at the Knezevo police station that people who had been killed at the Koricanske Stijene were people of Muslim ethnicity? " Your answer was: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the police station in Knezevo, after we returned from the scene, when the storm and rain had already started, then I knew it. Bosko Peulic, who was commander of the 22nd Brigade, told me and the captain who had filmed it told me and we standing in front of the camera made an appeal to everyone who knew anything, who survived, to come to us and we guaranteed their freedom. And that's how we found 14 survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, 13 survivors who were saved. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That happened the next day on the 23rd of August, when you returned to the scene; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd, when I came back, that's when I learned. On the 22nd, I had not yet managed to get to the crime scene. So I didn't know yet. How could I? It was still 30 kilometres away from me. They could have been Serbian victims. The separation line was not far from there, and the shells were falling all around. I can understand you putting questions to me in these comfortable conditions but you can't understand what I'm saying. I was working while a civil and a religious war was raging all around me. I was an investigating judge, and when an investigating judge conducts an on-site investigation, has to make personal observations [Realtime transcript read in error "objections"] to make conclusions. So on the 23rd, I knew it. On the 22nd, I didn't know it. I was informed there were two bodies originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You were told by Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic that the perpetrators had been civilian police and that there were -- and you understood there were one to two police on each bus in a convoy. That's what you understood on the 23rd; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd, I was told both by Peulic and the police structures, to put it that way, that the escort was made up of unknown people. Maybe they were policemen; maybe they were infiltrators. Now, I suspect, after all this time, that this crime at Koricanske Stijene, was no good to the Serbs. It was committed in order to later put all sorts of pressure on Republika Srpska. So I repeat, who would be crazy to cover up so many victims? Does a drug trafficker selling drugs do that publicly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, the question was not whether this crime was good or bad to the Serbs. The question was whether you were told that there had been civilian police on each bus. Did you know that or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know. I was told that there were infiltrators. Do you know what infiltrators means? That means men who had put on police uniforms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you just please concentrate on answering the question posed by the Prosecutor. Please continue, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure about this, but page 64, line 8, the witness said by direct "observation." Rather than personal "objection." He said: The investigating judge can make conclusions only by direct observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree with it, Mr. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By direct observation? Well, that's the main role of the investigative judge. Those are the basic principles, regardless of what kind of legal system you're working in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Can we look at e-court page 56 in the English and page 49 in the B/C/S, at the top of the B/C/S page and the bottom of the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, this relates to what Mr. Peulic told you. The question was: "Now I want you to please try to remember his exact words. When he said that the people who committed this crime were, did he say they were military police from Prijedor, Sanski Most, or Novi Grad, or did he say just the policemen from either of those three municipalities? Your answer was: "I want to explain that to you as well, so that you don't have to waste any time. They were the police who were escorting the convoys. Each bus -- on each such bus there was one or two policemen who escorted such convoys, and for your information, it will make things easier for you, they were in blue uniforms. The military persons, army, they were wearing SMB olive-grey uniforms or camouflage uniforms." Then you were asked: "Did Mr. Peulic say that they were in blue uniforms, the policemen?" Your answer was: "Well, he said that they were civilian police. It wasn't the military police. It's a very simple thing, a very simple matter for me. One word is enough. That's why, I mean, he wanted them to be arrested." Now, he didn't tell you anything about infiltrators. You certainly didn't report that in this interview in 2001, did you?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see how one action and one conversation can lead to confusion and misunderstanding. Of course, I know what happened. And you believe this policeman from Pakistan, that he really wrote all this accurately and that it has to be the way he puts it. Mr. President, Peulic, the commander, and I, did talk. And at that time in our country there were all sorts of uniforms, including a variety of police uniforms. It's true that those were not military uniforms, but among police uniform there was a variety. So a person who is normally on guard duty could put on a different uniforms and go out to work as a policeman. Later, as time passed, we kept thinking who could have been infiltrated to do this, and with what motives. It's true when the Prosecutor says that in one vehicle there were two policemen, and in another vehicle only one, but we didn't know from what area. It was assumed they were from the area mentioned by the Prosecutor. We assumed but didn't know for sure. And Bosko Peulic also had his own assumptions that these people were from these areas and wore a variety of uniforms. As time passed and we tried to reconstruct event by event, we came to the conclusion that this was done by somebody who wanted to portray Serbs as criminals. It was no good. It did no good to the serious leadership or -- or normal people. Who could it have served? Ivankovic, for instance, and some other people, they robbed those people and killed them. Nobody among the Serbian people in Republika Srpska justified this crime. Everybody agrees about the same conclusion. And I don't know why the Prosecutor here is trying to catch me out in certain inconsistencies and he had sent me this Pakistani investigator who is not my equal. I am looking you in the eyes now and you can take my measure right here and now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I must let you know that this is not what this investigator wrote. I think this is an audiotape recorded at the time of your interview. Am I correct in so understanding, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we still have that tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we may, before the break, if Your Honour agrees, if we can give the witness a copy of his -- the B/C/S version of the transcript to review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any difficulty with that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer do you expect the --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would estimate approximately 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.15. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could quickly raise what would normally be a housekeeping matter but now because of the imminent appearances of the witness has some greater urgency. We, that is the Prosecution, made a motion quite some time ago to exclude a portion of Mr. Jaksic's testimony. We have no record of a decision on that motion. I believe the Defence doesn't either, so unless we missed something, apparently that's still pending and I wanted to raise it before the witness appeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Chamber is considering the issue. Yes, Mr. File. You said you would need 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you try to conclude it in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I will try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, did you have the opportunity to locate any part of the transcript of your 2001 interview where you feel you were abused or pressured into giving false testimony?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I looked at this, as far as I could, and it turns out as if this was all milk and honey as we say in popular language. Ten hours of interrogation, interruption, abuse, and then going back and forth to receive instructions, and I know who he received instructions from. Look here, what's the reason for not putting a question to me now but going back to precisely what I said was wrong with it. A policeman came, and I told him the truth. First of all, this individual was not prepared for many of these facts. Second of all, in many of these issues, we see that I say one thing, it's mathematically correct, and he say it is mathematically incorrect. This is what I'm going to say to you now. This is quite clear, there is no reason for me to say otherwise. I spoke the truth. Only Jesus Christ is infallible. I make mistakes, other people make mistakes, but I do acknowledge my mistakes. So to put it quite simply, it transpires from this that everything was excellent and all in good order. It wasn't. This man was shouting at me. He asked me about two individuals, Muslims, Filipovic and somebody else, because he was a relative of one of the politicians. So that's why this individual came to put questions to me, and he wouldn't ask me any questions about 10.000 victims of my own people and other peoples. Let me tell you quite simply, I was born in the village of Bistrica. It's 60 kilometres away from Jasenovac, 50 kilometres away from Kozara. If I may finish, please. This is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I'm cutting you off. Do you remember the question? If you can answer the question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He asked me if what I said there was the result of any sort of duress and I'm answering by saying that there was harassment. Scientifically speaking, not everyone is capable of putting questions, not everyone is capable of answering questions, and not everyone is capable of following or observing things happening over a long period of time. There was this individual who came and put questions to me. And that's my answer to you. Ask me now and -- and I'll answer. And the Trial Chamber will seek -- hear clearly what I have to say. And a moment ago you interrupted me when I was about to say the most important of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please listen carefully to the question and concentrate on answering the question. I will ask Mr. File to ask his question again, if necessary. Please continue, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We're going to move on to the amount of time -- I just want to clarify the amount of time that you spent on the scene at Koricanske Stijene. At transcript page 56, lines 20 to 24 today, you said that you were on the scene for two hours, from 1500 to 1700 hours, and that you were never on the scene any longer than that. Dr. Karadzic intervened and added that it was four hours. But the correct answer was that you were there for two hours; right?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was four hours. Between 1300 hours and 1700 hours. So that would be four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I think that his Excellency Mr. Kwon sensed why I intervened. I heard four hours having been said, and what was recorded in the transcript was two hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, regardless of who is asking what, the answer is four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After -- you want to say something after Mr. Karadzic says something, please wait. Put a pause between his -- his words and your words, in light of the interpretation that is going on. Do you follow? Yes, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat this now for the sake of everyone. The correct answer is four hours, regardless of who puts the question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at the same document that is on the screen, the transcript of your interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: English page 50; B/C/S page 44, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You'll see towards the bottom half of the page in English you are saying: "After the rain, and because it was cold, it was already getting dark and you know that in the mountains days are shorter. And I told you that we stayed there for about two hours. During that period, two civilians came..." And it goes on. You see that?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see that. Where is that? Do you have that cursor to show it to me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 9 and 10 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I arrived at the scene, was around two hours. Well, you see, this was an on-site investigation. I calculated in the amount of time I spent there the time when we were trying to find shelter from the rain. There was a storm and a shower. Nobody could stay outdoors, so I factored in also the time spent in Knezevo when we appealed over the TV for all those who knew anything about it to report to the nearest police station. So there -- they were four hours in all, because I considered that to be part of the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You said in paragraph 9 of your statement that -- we're talking about your witness statement now: "I could not be present there due to other obligations except on 23 August 1992 in the afternoon because I was the only investigating judge and had to attend other investigations every half-hour or hour." But my question to you is: What other case could possibly have been more important than this massacre of 200 civilians such that you would never return to the scene again, other than this two-hour visit to the crime scene or four-hour visit to the area?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question is logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. What objection is it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that 120 is a -- a horrible enough figure, and I kindly appeal to the Prosecutor not to inflate it thus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You said the question was logical. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said that the question was logical. The only thing I did was conduct an on-site investigation as a preliminary investigative action. Since there were between 165 and 170 victims, if you're asking me to give you precise figures, we could -- arrived at that number on the basis of the number of the buses, the seats on the buses, and the space available for them to be standing. Of course any victim is a victim too much. But we concluded that on the basis of the vehicle used, it could have been between 165 and 170 persons. That was on the basis of the type of the bus, carrying capacity, and similar. As for your logical question, I carried out the on-site investigation only. But this was the situation: Every hour, there were cases of hand-grenades being thrown at different facilities and buildings and this was just one investigative action. That's to say, the crime scene was filmed on a camera. The survivors were called upon to report to the nearest station over the TV. There was a separation line, a confrontation line quite nearby, and an order was issued on the following day to an individual called Markovic and Vodovnik to attend the scene so that autopsies may be carried out and the identification process completed. So this was about preliminary investigative actions. But there were many cases of hand-grenades being held, buildings in Banja Luka being torched, et cetera. Whereas, this was just a -- a crime scene examination. I wasn't in charge of an investigation, and I keep repeating this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, then, let's return to what happened at that crime scene. You had a crime scene technician named Milivoje Pavicic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: One of the technicians, he was a junior technician, the technician in charge was Branko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the family name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another technician was Radovan Sukalo, also an experienced technician. The other one was Srdjan Oljaca. This Pavicic was not the person who would, in fact, be examining crime scenes. He was carrying bags around, to put it quite frankly. At the time I was working, I didn't know the scale of the civilian and religious war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: My question was: You had a crime scene technician named Milivoje Pavicic. That was it. All that required --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Pavicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: All that required was a yes as an answer. Now I would like to direct your attention to a signed witness statement from this individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 25183. Now, if we go to page 4, paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have it in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I don't believe we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Here you'll see that he is referring to September, ten days after the initial -- I'm just going to read to you the relevant portions. We're talking about a visit to the site again, in paragraph 12, in September. In paragraph 14 it says: "The lower court investigating judge did not come." The part that I'm interested in is on the next page, paragraphs 16 and 17. Here it says: "The men from Prijedor wearing the rubber suits began pulling out the bodies so they could be loaded on a crane. They were put on a wooden platform which was suspended on the crane. I saw that, two by two, bodies were lifted twice and then the crane broke down. I recorded this with video camera. I came back up to the road and continued to record the crime scene when the chief of the Prijedor public security station Simo Drljaca, started yelling at me for filming the site. He asked me who ordered me to film, and I said Chief Buhovac. He ordered me to stop recording the scene. I did not record anything else that day and they stopped pulling out the bodies because the crane broke. I think they could only remove four bodies during the first day. During the four days that I was around Drljaca, he was saying things like: I was in Belgrade and I wasn't around. I think Buhovac was there as well when Drljaca was saying. I did not believe him due to the fact that he ordered me to stop shooting the scene which should have been proper procedures. "We went background to Knezevo where I, Brane Buhovac, Zdenko Tesanovic [phoen] and Srdjan Oljaca waited for a few more days to see whether identification would take place. The rest of the team went back to Banja Luka the same date. I have been asked why Simo Drljaca, the chief of the Prijedor police SJB, would be at the scene. I can only say that we all knew that it was the Prijedor police who had done this crime and that's why Drljaca was present." My question for you is: Surely you worked closely enough with your crime scene technician that you were aware that these things were happening at the crime scene in September; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, now you have heard what this man asked me and since I'm not entitled to give or many any comments, let me tell you this. This man Pavicic whom he mentioned was a young man. This is the first time I'm seeing this, and I don't believe that this is what he said, unless he was insane. He is asking me about something that I did not absolutely witness. I said that was there on -- one day only, on the 22nd of August, 1992, at the crime scene, and he is describing something that happened in the month of September. And this individual was either given money or was insane. He draws Radovan Karadzic into this story. Let me tell you quite clearly that this is crime against the Serbian people, and only if he turned insane would Radovan Karadzic have done this. Let's compare this to whether Obama would have supported what had been done to those children last year. We see that among the technician, there is was Radovan Sukalo, Velko Maric, Srdjan Oljaca, Branko Buhovac. So how can Pavicic carry more statement in his statement than his superior, Branko Buhovac. This statement was either the result of a bribe or -- or something else, and this is the first time I hear of this. And I would always keep repeating this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Mr. Jankovic, where in this statement, in particular in those that were read to you, this crime technician, Mr. Pavicic, was drawing Mr. Karadzic into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Paragraph 13, Mr. President. But he wasn't drawing him into it in a negative way. But he does mention in paragraph 13 Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will leave it at that. Yes, please continue. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. File will ask you questions. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's important for me to tell you this. This is good for our general public to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. File will ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, Slobodan Avlijas came here to testify for the Defence and he confirmed that there was a meeting on the 30th of August, attended by a number of high-ranking RS officials as well as some of your colleagues, including the presidents of the county courts and the public prosecutor, Mr. Panic, and here's what he said at transcript pages 35187 to 35188. He said: "Let's not reinvent the wheel here. The entire RS knows that it was done by members of the SJB in Prijedor commanded by Simo Drljaca." He went on to say: "It is no secret at all and it was known on that day of the meeting the entire Krajina and all of the RS knew that the police station or SJB, I'm not sure of the exact name at the time, was in charge of escorting a civilian convoy, a convoy of civilian population, I think predominantly of Muslim ethnicity." He continued: "There was no doubt about whether or not the crime had been committed or not. Everything was known." Finally he said: "If it had been a well functioning state, Simo Drljaca should have been locked up. If there is command responsibility in a well functioning state, then there can be no discussion about it." Now, Mr. Jankovic, senior officials in the RS knew who was responsible. Your colleagues on the court knew who was responsible. The prosecutor knew who was responsible. Surely you must have known as the investigating judge where to go looking for the perpetrators of this crime; right?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not right. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Before you do, I want to ask you whether you ever summoned anyone from the Prijedor police to answer questions about this incident. You didn't do that, did you?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I've told you this for 100 times now, that the only thing I did was the on-site investigation as part of the preliminary investigative action. And I made an attempt at having autopsies conducted. I could not have summoned anyone because I didn't know their names. A witness who was arrested, Darko, I can't recall his name at present, I didn't know who the perpetrators were. There was guess-work. I agree with you. People were guessing but didn't know precisely who they were. As I said, a killer is always in hiding, as is a drug dealer, an adulter, et cetera. Nobody wanted to hush this up except for the perpetrators, of course. But we didn't know at the time -- was the scale of the war. If you go back to the time when I was proceeding in this case, and this was also a question put to me by this unfortunate investigator from Pakistan. I had a pen and a notepad with me and he asked me why I didn't arrest those men who had a tank. I would have been a super -- superman had I been able to do that. I would dearly like to have seen you there with me to see what you would have done in my shoes. I will never say this. I have never said this. I -- I do not justify this at all. Every human life it precious and this is something that was a burden for the Serbian people. Nobody tried to conceal this. Unfortunately, we had a -- a stretch of the front line of 2.000 kilometres, and unfortunately, we were short of a genocide having been committed there, and had all of this not happened I would not be here today. But go on, say what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to return to 65 ter 25926 and look at your transcript again, at English page 69 B/C/S page 59. Okay. Here you were asked -- you said: "First, the only entity or a person who was capable of identifying and arresting perpetrators was the civilian police. The civilian police and nobody else. Whether they were willing or not, that's another issue, another question." Then you were asked: "But couldn't you have found out -- found that out if you talked to Stojan Zupljanin who was the head of the civilian police?" Your answer was: "No, because I did not talk to him after... about it." Then you were asked: "Was that because -- let's be honest here, because the police were involved and it would have been dangerous for you to push the identification and arrest the perpetrators?" And your answer was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we get the next page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your answer was: "Not only for me, for everybody."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: "Every policeman at the time was the force or power." That was what you said in 2001, and that was the truth, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I said something different. Perhaps, I mean, in reaching a conclusion. I mean, well, I repeat, yet again. Few people are capable of putting the right questions. So then and now, and always, I can just tell you that I, as a civilian investigating judge, could not have arrested a policeman. So the sequence was that I would submit a record and then the prosecutor could ask for identification from the police. You see, here people really didn't know because uniforms were different. They didn't know for a long time who the perpetrators were. Now people found out who the perpetrators were and they were prosecuted before the judiciary of the BH. Now, what is there here that you don't know or don't want to know? Some judges and prosecutors in order to establish the prosecutor's office of the BH and the court of BH, they saw themselves here and then they kept this in a drawer. Vojkan Dimitrijevic was here and defended a person, a suspect, and you never asked him whether he knew and what he knew. He returned and became a judge of the high court in contravention of all international codes, and conversely he said --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't want to hear the truth. That's the problem. I wish you all the best. You just do your job.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You saw Simo Drljaca four or five days after your investigation was complete, and he told you: "You finished your job. You submitted it. You surrendered it to the SUP. You are -- you shouldn't be dealing with it anymore." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that was at the Bosna hotel. It was private, not official. No, I knew Simo. We were on good terms, I knew many people, Simo included. Regardless of whether somebody is a good person or a bad person I cannot avoid that. But speaking personally -- I mean, but, no, not officially. No way. I didn't know Simo's role in this case for a very long time, until I went to the BH court. And you simply don't want to look at the transcript of my interview before the BH court. Many prosecutors and judges were promoted by falsely presenting different cases, including this one, Mr. President. So this one is included.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That interview with the BH court or your statement in front of the BH court, that happened in 2008. And that is the moment when justice began --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: -- to be done in this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Yes, precisely. Now this is the right question. The only right question you have put to me so far. So this could have been dealt with. And you didn't ask me about that. There was this dispatch of the president of the republic, there was this dispatch from the minister of the interior and who was accused here, poor man, for nothing. And that was stolen. They were waiting for the establishment of the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina on orders from The Hague Tribunal, and then can you imagine this wonderland where out of 100 persons 90 to 95 are being prosecuted? So out of 100 person there, 90 to 95 persons are being prosecuted, belonging to one ethnicity only. So they were waiting. Some of them did know. And that's why I have this suspicious regarding these foreign intelligence services. Some people knew. And according to the law and the constitution, this prosecutor's office cannot exist in such a way. And if I'm a legalist, and indeed I am, in 1991, I acted -- no, sorry, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I was supposed to -- no, just a moment, please. I was supposed -- I'm saying this for the Trial Chamber not for you. I was supposed to know what would happen in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm asking you to answer the question. Yes [Overlapping speakers] Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about another suspicion that you have which you state in paragraph 11 where you say that you later established -- this is your statement. You later establish that: "For reasons I do not know, video material and these two dispatches went missing. This made me suspect that there was a conspiracy afoot by persons unknown."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to look at 65 ter 25166, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: When this comes up, what you will see is that this is an Official Note dated 5th October, 1999, of the interview of Branko Buhovac, the head of the forensic department of the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You'll see towards the very bottom it says: "As for the videotape of the scene, I can tell you that it has been erased using a VCR on the order of the UKP chief, Goran Macar." Now, in the same ICTY signed witness statement from Mr. Pavicic, you see a similar description in paragraphs 16 to 17. So my question is: Were you aware of the possibility that this tape may have been erased on the orders of someone inside the government?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand you. Again, an excellent question, and I'm glad for the sake of my own public. I personally doubt that Buhovac wrote this. This Pavicic, he would be prone to do anything. And I'm glad that this will be heard here. Goran Macar on his order, no. Now, what is it that happened? When there was this take-over of the police in Banja Luka with the assistance of SFOR, one police came and another police left. Then the police broke into the crime investigation service and then they took everything. You know, they're policemen. They don't know what things are. They just take everything. Now on these slides, that's the technical term, you can see all the pictures of Koricanske Stijene. I saw all of that, I was shown all of that. I don't know what you're trying to say by putting this. I don't know Goran Macar and I really doubt that he could have ordered this. So this was kept in the crime prevention service and then SFOR broke in and took everything. And also 54/92, Mico Stanisic's telegram, and also President Karadzic dispatch, all of that was stolen. And I know why, so that people could later get certain positions. Now what you're asking me now that's a good question. That was not just erased. It cannot be erased. There are five witnesses who signed this in my office number 29. Where they were, what they did, how they barely survived. I mean, it defies belief how they survived. Now would somebody come and erase the slides? When live people are saying what happened. Your question is not logical. I cannot give you an answer in terms of something that somebody else had done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's good for our public that this question was put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript does not reflect that his record 354 also went missing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's 554?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or 554.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you mentioned Mico Stanisic. I'd like to look at --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: -- his statement in this case, draft statement, which is 1D9900, at paragraphs 57 to 59.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: All of this is empty. I cannot see a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Pardon me, 56 to 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Here, as you'll see, it says: "An investigative judge was assigned to the case and took statements from victims. A criminal report against unknown perpetrators was filed on 8 September, 1992. On 11 September, 1992, CSB Chief, Stojan Zupljanin, ordered the Prijedor SJB to take full written statements from policemen involved in this incident and provide him with other information needed to identify the perpetrators. Exhibit D3763 is the communication sent by Zupljanin. "Once an investigative judge had taken charge of the investigation, the obligation of the Ministry of Interior to investigate ceased, subject to any orders of that investigating judge." Now this statement appears to be blaming you for the lack of any further action on this investigation. So my question is: Do you accept blame for the failure to identify and prosecute any perpetrators during the war?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us finally agree on something. By formally interpreting what you read out, yes, I'm the one to be blamed. But in real terms, how could I identify a policeman? I'm asking all of you. I'm asking myself. In simple terms, an investigative judge just carried out an investigative action which was an attempt to carry out an on-site investigation and an autopsy and also he interviewed five persons in his office because he didn't know what would happen afterwards. At the time when this action was taken, the size was not known or the scale was not no known. To identify these persons it only could have been done by somebody who had force. Not somebody who had a notebook. Do you understand what I'm saying? Now it's different in peacetime. But, at that time, it could have been done only by someone who had force. If I had force, wearing civilian clothes and carrying a notebook - do you understand what I'm saying? - then that would be logical but this is the first time I see this. If we were to look at all this, then the conclusion would be different...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I just have a couple of remaining questions about the cases that you describe in your statement that you claim in paragraph 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could bear with me just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. File, please conclude in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In your statement, you refer to a number of cases that you claim show that you worked on the basis of the law and regularly tried Serbs who committed crimes against non-Serbs. I don't have time to cover all of these cases right now, but I'd like to look at one of the ones that you mention, which is 1D55188. I don't have -- I haven't seen that there's been a translation uploaded so we've translated just a couple of pages of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could have number 25887, please. And as this comes up, in your statement, you say that this case file of Vedran Mandic clearly indicates that they were tried for crime against non-Serbs in Banja Luka and at the end they were killed on the attack on the Medjan police station. Now if you look at this Official Note from the CSB, this tells a story of Mr. Mandic sitting down in a police car after asking to speak with two police inspectors and telling him that he has heard the police are asking questions around town about him and his activities in the SOS, and he says: "In early April 1992, I heard from some friends that SOS special units would be established in Banja Luka but also in other towns. Volunteers were sought who would work in groups to defend the Serbian people. One of the tasks was opposing the JNA which wanted to take away weapons and leave the Serbs without the possibility of defence and the second task was to drive Muslims, Croats and Albanians out of town. "I don't want to talk much about the establishment of SOS units. Everything was done in secret. Ringo and Panto talked to me at Laus and later I met Nenad Stevandic." Then he goes on to say: "From that day on, as a member of the SOS I did as Panto, Ringo, and Stevandic ordered. "And what were those orders?" He says: "They told to us destroy buildings belonging to Muslims and other ethnic groups who are against the Serbs and to intimidate them to move out of the area." Then as the statement goes on, he complains that he spent a lot of his own money on weapons and explosives, and he says: "When I compare how much money I have spent it is clear that all this is not profitable for me. Everyone knows who will benefit from our attempts to drive out Balijas. Those people will seize their shops and houses and we will have nothing." Then later he goes on to describe how he deals drugs to pay for some of these explosives. So my -- my question is - because he is released after this, he just leaves - don't you think that this is sort of the moment where the police would want to arrest this person?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: May I? May I answer? Well, it's a good things that you read this out for the sake of our own public and least of all for the Tribunal to have these facts known. It is a fact that this man was killed during the attack on the police station. It is a fact that Goran Bijelic was killed then, a person from the DB, a Serb. To this day, no light has been shed on that. Now, as for these persons, I know of them but I don't know what they did. I don't know who compiled this. It wasn't this way. That would be it, as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: And just another thing - just a moment, please - it's very important for all. So we all lived together. The old Muslims were good people. Had it not been for foreign interference none of this would have happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you're not answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead. Please say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please listen to the questions put to you by Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. I will now answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a good thing for the sake of our public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. We are not conducting this trial for the benefit of the public. This is a serious criminal trial against Mr. Radovan Karadzic. You are not assisting the Chamber. Please. Please listen to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we please look at number 25929, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is going to be, when it comes up, another Official Note that describes what happened regarding the attack at the police station. And here you see this was not in connection with the police attempting to pursue this individual for criminal activities against Muslim businesses that he was perpetrating during this time. It says that: "He approached the police station with dynamite and that he had come to blow us up, because, as he put it, who had given us the right to bring in his pregnant wife to the police station. Since I smelled alcohol on his breath, I tried to talk to him nicely and explain to him that his wife had been stopped by the military police as she was found to be driving a Lada Niva car without number plates and a corresponding car registration card. I also told him that the policemen had treated his wife very courteously. However, Vedran began to insult the police, saying we were chicken shits and that we should go to Motike and arrest Ustashas and not his wife. I'm not going to read out the entire report, but Vedran then leaves. The police try to call the special detachment for back up, then he returns later with the rifle grenade and he is confronted by the police and is killed in a shoot-out." And the report also indicates as a side note that the police were aware he had been conducting bombings all over the city, not because they had any intent to arrest him, but, it says: "I am mentioning all of this to show that in view of his activities up to that moment, there was a real threat to safety of the members of the police." So what this document actually shows is that the police were well aware of his activities. They were not trying to arrest him. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I have to tell you this is the first I hear of this. How can I give an answer when this is the very first time I hear of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, Mr. President. I don't think Mr. File is respecting the Trial Chamber's time-limits at all, and I also don't think this is a particularly important area of examination. So I think you should terminate the direct -- the cross-examination and let -- let us finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he is coming to an end. Yes, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am coming to the end, and I would just actually -- well, first of all, I would point out that this comes from the Defence exhibit 1D55188.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That wasn't admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It was referred to in the witness's witness statement as clearly indicating that these individuals were tried for crimes against non-Serbs and that they were killed in the attack on this police station. And as evidence that they worked on the basis of law. So this goes to the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm following you. Did you mean to say that you tender this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I -- I will tender this document when this is completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was whether you are coming to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said you are -- you meant to tender some documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes. I would tender the pages of the transcript that we've referred to. I may have to verify that with the Registrar to ensure that we have the correct page references in the final version of the transcript that's uploaded in e-court. But I would tender those pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the future, I would like the Prosecutor to tender as -- as we go on. Yes. And? The intercept -- the transcript pages we -- we dealt with. And what else?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Actually, I think that's -- that's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think they should identify them to us by e-mail, and we'll get back to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll assign a number for that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 25926 will be Exhibit P6609.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. But I hope it won't take too long. So could we immediately call up this transcript of the interview? I don't really have the number here right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P6609.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please. Mr. Jankovic, I'd like to clear up where you worked and from where, what did you say, from -- on this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page in Serbian and probably in English too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at line 7. Is it true that you said that from 1988, you were investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You see? Your Honours, it would never cross my mind to say something that is not true. Here I just got it wrong, in terms of dates. And I have all the papers to prove when I finished higher school, law school, when I became investigating judge. Of course, I knew it better at that time. I am able to say exactly how long I worked as a judge, when I was replaced, and by whom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are just particulars, details, that everybody forgets with time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this page 4? Yes, look at line 19. Year 1977 is mentioned. We had understood that you became judge then; but, in fact, it's the year when you returned to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I returned to Banja Luka in 1977. I couldn't be judge because I was then a student at the high school of criminology until 1985. That's true. And thank you for asking this. I repeat, I just made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 5. 14 in English. It says here you worked as crime investigation inspector until 1988.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly true, in the crime department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add these pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 7. 7. The numbering of pages is different, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the top of the page, you explain differences in the system.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Between the Anglo-Saxon system and continental law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did that occur as a problem in your mutual understanding?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: A major problem. And you heard today preliminary investigative actions are not the same as investigation, as the Prosecutor persistently tries to present it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender pages 7 and 8 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure we are seeing the corresponding pages; in particular, between the B/C/S and English --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, it's 7. And I'm moving onto 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, we'll add these two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll leave this document. Let us look at 65 ter 25183.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were shown a passage from the statement of this gentleman, Pavicic, or a few passages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you if these allegations made here --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this page 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, it says like this: [In English] "Knezevo with the following personnel: Gordana Radujko, a public prosecutor; Judge Jevto Jankovic; an inspector from CSB whom I don't recall his name. We came to the public security station in Knezevo to get further instructions, as we were not familiar with the area?" [Interpretation] Is this consistent with the truth?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it isn't. And for the sake of our public, it's good you ask this question. I never went anywhere with Gordana Radujko. This investigation was done by Djordje Dujicic [phoen] or this Pavkovic simply made this up. There is no third possibility.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Both speakers are kindly asked to observe a pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, he mentions Peulic and so on: [In English] "Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic was concerned about the incident and told us that there had been a survivor found. I believe that Judge Jevto Jankovic told me to take a video-recorded statement from the survivor." [Interpretation] Did you ask that everything be filmed?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm hearing this for the first time. This little Pavlicic could not have approached Bosko Peulic and talk to him. He wasn't able to talk even to Jevto Jankovic. And it was -- it's not possible that I gave him as, an outsider, any orders. I could have given instructions only to Radovan Sukalo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch all the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This man either took money to say this, or he is completely crazy. Or this is a forgery. There is no other way. You'll see, the truth will out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch all the names. But did -- were you the one who ordered that everything be documented?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't order him anything. He was a pipsqueak. He was insignificant. Yes, I did give orders to Orljaca, Sukalo, and the third one, Buhovac. People who know about this will laugh. The man who survived is called Midhat Mujkanovic. A soldier brought him and said, Here, we found one survivor. At that point, I still didn't know what the scale of this civil/religious war would be. And the survivor asks me, Are you going to kill me? I said no. I put him in my own car. We took him to the hospital. I later questioned him in my office at the court, and he got out through the organisation, Merhamet. And now he is still alive, thank God. But I cannot explain this because foreign intelligence services are ruling Bosnia-Herzegovina, this country of miracles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 4, please. I'll read from paragraph 13 in English: [In English] "I should mention some rumours that I heard that during this time about Radovan Karadzic. We heard that Karadzic had ordered that the bodies that were at Koricanske Stijene were to be recovered and that the incident was clearly a crime. There was never the atmosphere amongst us that Simo Drljaca had done a good job (in killing the Muslims)." [Interpretation] Did you hear at the scene that I had already sent certain messages to Knezevo regarding this incident?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I've said this a hundred times. This is a crime that blemishes Serbian people. And Karadzic was not out to prejudice Serbian people. Even if he were completely crazy, he wouldn't order something like this. I told you what happened. And you will see. Nothing could happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina without foreign intelligence services. Prosecutor Tieger, please pay attention to what I'm saying. There was a clear plan to portray one side as the only culprit, the criminal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the number. Mr. Karadzic is overlapping with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D4236. 4236 has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But since the translation is wrong, please read slowly the text so our interpreters can translate it. And tell us also how this document is related to your evidence about your powers and your duties? The Serbian version, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we remove the English so that interpreters could interpret from Mr. Jankovic's words.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this as just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will take a look into the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. We have -- we have -- we have them in e-court. I think -- What's the basis of your objection, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll withdraw it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Was this part of the associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was admitted a long time ago. In some other case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is what we admitted at the beginning of this witness's evidence as part of associate exhibit, I take it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could read out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Lower court in Banja Luka, 24 September 1992. To the basic public prosecutor, Banja Luka. Attention: Deputy Marinko Kovacevic. Having conducted the preliminary investigating procedures." You have to believe me, Mr. President, I mentioned this in 1992. Why wouldn't I mention it in 2014? So: "Having conducted the preliminary investigating procedures, upon the request from your file, KTM 2293/92 dated 14 September 1992, we are returning to you the file for the public prosecutor to make his decision. We emphasise that out of the possible seven persons, we have questioned five persons whose statements are identical. So I believe that questioning the remaining two who are seriously injured and are undergoing treatment is pointless. Hereby we make available to you the entire file."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I draw everyone's attention to the fact that in the English translation the reference is to investigation, not to preliminary investigating procedures, which is important. What does this mean, Mr. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor needs to ask the police to identify possible perpetrators of the Koricanske Stijene killings. An investigation can start only when perpetrators are known. This was just an on-site investigation, and there the whole procedure hit a snag.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness needs to repeat the last thing. He is speaking much too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreters were not available to catch up with you. Could you -- could you repeat from the beginning [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... if I may, Your Excellencies, my question is not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this mean: "We are returning for you the file for the public prosecutor to make a decision." It's interpreted well. So you returned this for the prosecutor to make further decisions. Please briefly and slowly answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It means, quite simply, the prosecution had to ask for the perpetrators of the Koricanske Stijene killings to be identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: And when they are identified, when they are known, a request has to be made by the prosecution to conduct an investigation. Only then could the investigation start. Not at this moment when nobody, including the prosecutor, knows who they are, at the stage of on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which five persons out of the possible seven did you hear? Who are these people?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'll tell you now exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't need the names. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Ordinary mortals. Bakrija Jakupovic, Sulejman Kahrimanovic, Emsud Garibovic, Midhet Mujanovic. The latter was the one whom I brought in my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I'm just asking are they victims or perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: These are survivors. Those who survived the massacre. Only God could have saved them. No one short of God.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, did you ever notice, did you have any indication or information that anybody from the authorities, be it central or local authorities, did not wish the perpetrators to be identified and caught?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I did not. And I tried to explain it in my own words. Only a fool who wishes evil upon Republika Srpska could have done that. Because all these people were on the list, and the list was in the hands of the UNPROFOR, the ICRC, the Muslims as a party to the conflict, the Croats as a party to the conflict, and we had a copy of the list. Nine buses set out accompanied with these lists, and three failed to arrive. Even during a genocide, somebody survives. So it couldn't be hidden. If I had known about this, I would have dropped everything to identify these persons. If I had known that in 2014 this would be a case before The Hague Tribunal, we would have identified and apprehended all these people. These are our criminals whom you should not under estimate, by the way, in cahoots with foreign intelligence services. Somebody needed to do this for their own political aims. It was certainly not to the advantage of the Serbian leadership and our people. This is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something to the president of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague. Now you are free to go. Please [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that the truth will prevail. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm coming back to the point you raised earlier on today. I was confused -- I was confused with the pending motion before the Tribunal; that is, with respect to KW426. But your point was with respect to Dusko Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that issue was resolved by Mr. Robinson's e-mail on the same date which was sent to parties at 7.04 p.m. on 16th -- 25th of June, in which Mr. Robinson said -- I will quote: "We will delete the paragraphs in question from the final statement of the witness." So --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The confusing part is caused by the fact that that wasn't followed up, and I presume Mr. Robinson will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it the revised version of the statement has yet to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. And it will be, Mr. President. Thank you for calling that to my attention because I completely forgot about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tomorrow we will begin with General Mladic's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then the format, the Scheduling Order -- it will -- if it lasts more than a day, it will -- we will hear from him just for one session and continue to the day after?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's our proposal, Mr. President, that we hear from him between 9.00 and 10.30, and then if we do not conclude his testimony, we resume his testimony at 9.00 the following day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any observation with respect to that, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We stand adjourned till tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 28th day of January, 2014, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.49 p.m.,
